questions.q: Your resolution agent must check customer account status and recent order history before acting on a case. The two lookups have no ordering dependency on each other, but the coordinator currently dispatches them as two sequential subagent calls, and high case volume is making that round-trip latency a real bottleneck. What's the most effective fix?
options: Merge both lookups into a single combined subagent that performs both investigations in one turn
Emit both Task calls within a single coordinator response so the two subagents run concurrently, then collect both results before proceeding
Add a batching layer that packs multiple subagent invocations into one API request
Increase max_tokens so each lookup resolves faster
questions.explain:
Emitting both Task calls within a single coordinator response is what actually runs the two subagents concurrently; merging them into one subagent loses the modularity of separate investigations, and neither a generic batching layer nor a bigger token budget changes the fact that the calls are currently dispatched sequentially. Current docs: the Task tool is now named Agent; Task remains an alias.
Not “Merge both lookups into a single combined subagent that performs bo…” — Merging the lookups into one subagent loses the modularity of separate investigations, and it does not run two subagents side by side.
Not “Add a batching layer that packs multiple subagent invocations into …” — A generic batching layer packs requests together but does not make the two independent subagent calls run concurrently from the coordinator.
Not “Increase max_tokens so each lookup resolves faster” — max_tokens limits output length. It does not change that the calls are dispatched one after another, which is the actual bottleneck.

questions.q: Your refund tool exposes refund_reason_code (an enum: "defective," "not_as_described," "customer_request," "policy_exception") and refund_justification (free text for additional context). Logs show the agent frequently stuffs long explanatory text into reason_code and leaves justification blank, even on cases where a bare code isn't enough detail for the finance team to evaluate. Both parameters already have descriptions. What's the clearest next fix?
options: Rename both parameters to something else entirely, on the theory that new names alone will resolve the confusion
Merge them into a single free-text refund_reason field and parse category and detail out of it server-side

Expand both parameter descriptions with concrete guidance: reason_code gets "must be exactly one of the enum values, never free text"; justification gets an example of what to write when the code alone doesn't capture enough context
Add a hook that rejects the call outright whenever justification is empty
questions.explain:
Concrete guidance in the description — exactly what belongs in the enum vs. what belongs in free text, with an example of when justification is actually needed — is the direct, lowest-effort fix for this kind of field-misuse pattern, ahead of renaming, merging the fields, or bolting on a rejection hook.
Not “Rename both parameters to something else entirely, on the theory th…” — Renaming parameters alone does nothing to clarify what belongs in the enum versus the free text, so the same misuse would continue.
Not “Merge them into a single free-text refund_reason field and parse …” — A single free-text field gives up the enum's structure and moves parsing to the server, which is a heavier fix for a simple description problem.
Not “Add a hook that rejects the call outright whenever justification …” — A rejection hook on empty justification forces text even when none is needed and does not teach the agent what belongs where.

questions.q: A customer disputes charges across three orders plus one account-level adjustment, requesting a $620 total refund. An initial lookup surfaces all four transaction amounts. After two subagents separately investigate return eligibility and account reconciliation, the synthesis step produces a final recommendation of "approve $105" — referencing the adjustment but dropping the three order amounts entirely, even though both subagents' own outputs were correct and complete. What's the most direct fix?
options: Increase the context window so intermediate results never need to be summarized
Maintain a persistent "case facts" block (each transaction ID and amount) carried alongside every prompt, outside the part of the conversation that gets condensed into a narrative summary
Re-run both subagent investigations at a higher temperature for more thorough coverage
Have the customer restate all four disputed amounts before the agent finalizes anything
questions.explain:
A persistent case-facts block carried outside the part of the conversation that gets condensed is what keeps specific numbers from disappearing during synthesis, which is exactly what happened to three of the four transaction amounts here. A bigger context window doesn't stop summarization from happening; higher temperature adds noise, not fidelity; and asking the customer to repeat themselves is a workaround, not a fix.
Not “Increase the context window so intermediate results never need to b…” — A larger context window does not prevent summarisation from happening, and the amounts were lost in condensing, not for lack of space.
Not “Re-run both subagent investigations at a higher temperature for mor…” — Higher temperature adds randomness rather than fidelity, so it would not keep the three order amounts in the final recommendation.
Not “Have the customer restate all four disputed amounts before the agen…” — Asking the customer to restate the amounts shifts the burden onto them and does not fix the loss of figures during synthesis.

questions.q: Your single general-purpose resolution agent handles returns, billing disputes, and account-security cases, with access to every relevant tool across all three areas. First-contact resolution varies sharply by category: returns succeed 88% of the time, billing disputes only 59%, and account-security cases are occasionally escalated based on insufficient identity verification depth. What's the most effective structural fix?
options: Give the single agent even more tools, including advanced financial-analysis and multi-factor-auth capabilities

Introduce a lightweight intake step that classifies each case and routes it to a specialized subagent per category (returns, billing, security), each scoped to only the tools relevant to its own case type
Keep one general agent, but add 15+ few-shot examples spanning all three case types
Split the system into three fully separate backend services, one per case type, with no shared coordinator at all
questions.explain:
Routing each case to a specialized subagent scoped to only its own category's tools directly addresses uneven performance across very different case types, without expanding any single agent's tool surface or relying on examples alone to cover three very different domains. Splitting into fully separate backend services throws away the shared coordinator without actually fixing tool scoping.
Not “Give the single agent even more tools, including advanced financial…” — Adding more tools to one agent increases its decision surface, which tends to worsen selection rather than improve uneven performance across categories.
Not “Keep one general agent, but add 15+ few-shot examples spanning all …” — Fifteen examples spread across three very different domains do not narrow the agent's tools, and the uneven results come from covering everything in one agent.
Not “Split the system into three fully separate backend services, one pe…” — Three entirely separate services with no coordinator removes the shared routing and oversight without solving how tools are scoped per case type.

questions.q: escalate_to_human is meant to always carry structured context (customer ID, root cause, attempted actions), and the system prompt says so explicitly and emphatically. Logs still show a meaningful share of escalations going out with minimal or blank context, and the coordinator doesn't stop them. What's the most direct, deterministic fix?
options: Make the system-prompt wording even stronger and more emphatic
Define escalate_to_human's input schema so customer_id, root_cause, and attempted_actions are required parameters the call cannot be made without
Add a hook that inspects the call after the fact and flags escalations with thin context for follow-up
Split escalate_to_human into two separate tools, one for routine escalations and one for emergencies
questions.explain:
Making the required fields part of the tool's own input schema means the call literally cannot be made without them — a deterministic guarantee that stronger prompt wording or a hook that only flags problems after the fact can't provide. Splitting the tool in two doesn't address the missing-context problem itself.
Not “Make the system-prompt wording even stronger and more emphatic” — Stronger wording is still advisory. The prompt already says this emphatically, yet escalations keep going out without context.
Not “Add a hook that inspects the call after the fact and flags escalati…” — A hook that only flags thin escalations afterward lets them go out first, so it does not prevent the missing context.
Not “Split escalate_to_human into two separate tools, one for routine …” — Splitting the tool into routine and emergency versions does nothing about the missing customer_id, root_cause and attempted_actions.

questions.q: Your written policy explicitly covers defective items (90-day window) and wrong items shipped (30-day window), but says nothing about unopened, resalable items returned outside either window — a real request that comes up in about 5% of cases. The agent currently escalates every one of these, which is dragging down first-contact resolution, even though the policy's spirit plausibly supports approving some of them. Under what condition should a case like this actually go to a human?
options: Whenever it involves more than one order or a large dollar amount
When the agent has genuinely run out of applicable policy to reason from — the request falls into real silence or ambiguity in the documented rules — and further tool calls won't resolve that gap
Once the agent has made at least three tool calls, since that indicates a thorough-enough investigation
Whenever sentiment analysis on the customer's message indicates frustration or urgency
questions.explain:
The right trigger for escalation is a genuine gap or silence in the documented policy that no further investigation can resolve on its own — not proxies like order count, dollar amount, tool-call count, or sentiment, all of which correlate poorly with whether the agent is actually equipped to decide the case.
Not “Whenever it involves more than one order or a large dollar amount” — Order count and dollar amount are proxies that do not show whether the policy covers the case, so they would send some solvable cases to humans.
Not “Once the agent has made at least three tool calls, since that indic…” — Tool-call count measures effort, not whether a policy gap exists, so it would escalate or hold cases for the wrong reasons.
Not “Whenever sentiment analysis on the customer's message indicates fru…” — Frustration or urgency does not indicate that policy is silent, so sentiment would escalate cases the agent can resolve.

questions.q: A pilot workflow needs three sequential checks — eligibility, account reconciliation, fraud assessment — where a red flag at any step should escalate immediately rather than continuing to the next step. The current coordinator runs all three regardless, and only checks for red flags once every step has already finished, wasting effort on cases that should have escalated at step one. What's the best fix?
options: Bake a rigid, fully-enumerated if-then-else decision tree directly into the coordinator's prompt
Have the coordinator inspect each subagent's result before dispatching the next one, and escalate immediately the moment a red flag appears, instead of always running the full sequence
Remove the subagent layer and have one agent call all the underlying tools directly with branching logic
Run all three checks in parallel, then escalate afterward if any of them raised a flag
questions.explain:
Checking each step's result before dispatching the next lets the coordinator escalate the moment a red flag appears, instead of always paying for every remaining step regardless of outcome. A rigid pre-baked decision tree is brittle against cases outside its exact enumerated conditions, and running everything in parallel doesn't save any of the wasted work this fix is meant to eliminate.
Not “Bake a rigid, fully-enumerated if-then-else decision tree directly …” — A rigid pre-written decision tree is brittle against cases outside its enumerated conditions and does not itself check results between steps.
Not “Remove the subagent layer and have one agent call all the underlyin…” — Removing the subagent layer in favour of one agent with branching logic gives up modular investigation without solving the early-exit problem.
Not “Run all three checks in parallel, then escalate afterward if any of…” — Running all three checks in parallel still pays for every check before any flag is acted on, so it saves none of the wasted work.

questions.q: A subagent tasked with verifying a customer's shipping address calls an address-validation tool twice; both attempts time out. It returns {"status": "complete", "findings": "Address verification unavailable"}. The coordinator reads this as "verification succeeded, address is fine" and proceeds to process the refund — but the address was actually wrong, and the shipment later fails. What's the core issue, and the fix?
options: The subagent's retry logic is too conservative; it should keep retrying until the backend eventually responds

The subagent needs a way to clearly distinguish "I investigated and got a definitive answer" from "I was unable to investigate at all," using a distinct status or explicit failure marker — so the coordinator can't mistake an inability to verify for a successful verification
Address validation is too unreliable to be part of this workflow and should be removed
The coordinator should automatically escalate any case where address data comes back unavailable
questions.explain:
The subagent needs a way to say "I could not verify this" that's structurally distinct from "I verified this and it's fine" — without that distinction, the coordinator has no way to avoid treating an inability to check as a clean pass. Retrying indefinitely doesn't solve the reporting problem, dropping the check loses real value, and blanket auto-escalation overcorrects for a problem that's really about signal clarity.
Not “The subagent's retry logic is too conservative; it should keep retr…” — Retrying until the backend responds could stall indefinitely, and it still would not tell the coordinator whether verification actually happened.
Not “Address validation is too unreliable to be part of this workflow an…” — Removing address validation loses real value. The issue is that a failure was reported as a completed check, not that the check exists.
Not “The coordinator should automatically escalate any case where addres…” — Escalating every case with unavailable address data overcorrects. The core problem is that the coordinator cannot tell failure from success.

questions.q: A complex billing dispute has two defensible outcomes given the exact same underlying facts (verified identity, order history, account status): a strict-policy calculation of $280, and a goodwill-exception calculation of $420. You want to reason through both paths independently — without one path's assumptions contaminating the other — but re-verifying the same facts from scratch in two completely separate sessions wastes backend calls and risks the two paths ending up with subtly inconsistent fact bases. What approach best threads this needle?
options: Stay in one session and add explicit labels at each step noting which path is currently being reasoned about
Run two entirely independent fresh sessions for the two paths, accepting the duplicated backend calls and the risk of drifting fact bases as an unavoidable cost

Branch into two isolated sessions from the same already-verified shared fact base, explore each path independently within its own branch, then bring both conclusions back together for a final recommendation
Have the agent keep detailed written notes and re-read them each time it switches between the two paths
questions.explain:
Branching from an already-verified shared fact base into two isolated explorations avoids both cross-contamination between the two paths (which a single shared session risks) and the wasted, potentially-inconsistent re-verification of two fully separate sessions. Manual labeling within one session or note-taking between path switches both rely on discipline rather than actual isolation.
Not “Stay in one session and add explicit labels at each step noting whi…” — Labelling steps inside one session still lets one path's assumptions colour the other. Labels depend on discipline rather than real isolation.
Not “Run two entirely independent fresh sessions for the two paths, acce…” — Two independent fresh sessions repeat the backend verification and may end up with inconsistent facts, which is the cost the team wants to avoid.
Not “Have the agent keep detailed written notes and re-read them each ti…” — Written notes re-read when switching paths leave both paths in one context, so assumptions can still leak between them.

questions.q: Your .claude/settings.json has a PreToolUse hook matching the Write tool that runs a validation script — exit code 0 for a valid file, exit code 2 for an invalid one. A developer's edit would produce a configuration file that fails that validation. What happens?
options: The file is written first, and the validation failure is only reported afterward
The write is blocked outright — the hook's exit code 2 prevents the tool call from executing at all
The hook only applies to Bash-style commands, so a Write call bypasses it entirely
The write proceeds regardless, since hooks are advisory rather than enforced
questions.explain:
A PreToolUse hook that exits with code 2 blocks the tool call outright, before it ever executes (other non-zero codes are non-blocking errors and the action goes ahead) — that's the entire point of the mechanism, not an advisory suggestion layered on top of it. The hook fires for the Write call regardless of file type (ruling out C), and the block happens before, not after, anything gets written (ruling out A and D).
Not “The file is written first, and the validation failure is only repor…” — A PreToolUse hook runs before the tool executes, so the file is not written first and validation is not merely reported afterwards.
Not “The hook only applies to Bash-style commands, so a Write call b…” — The hook matches the Write tool, so it applies to the write call and is not limited to Bash-style commands.
Not “The write proceeds regardless, since hooks are advisory rather than…” — Hooks are enforced, not advisory. Exit code 2 from a PreToolUse hook stops the tool call.

questions.q: A convention needs to apply consistently to API-related code scattered across several unrelated directory trees, not confined to one folder. A developer creates .claude/rules/api-validation.md with paths: ["src/api/**", "lib/api/**"]. Later, new code is added under server/api/handlers/. Does the existing rule apply there?
options: Yes — the presence of "api" anywhere in a path is enough to match
No — src/api/** and lib/api/** only match those two specific directory trees; a path like server/api/** needs to be added explicitly (or a broader pattern like **/api/** used instead)
Yes, but only once the new files have been committed to version control
No, because rules never apply to any directory that didn't exist when the rule file was first created
questions.explain:
Glob patterns are literal path matches: src/api/** and lib/api/** only cover those two specific trees, and a new directory like server/api/ needs to be added explicitly (or covered by a broader pattern such as **/api/**) — it isn't automatically included just because it also contains the word "api."
Not “Yes — the presence of "api" anywhere in a path is enough to match” — Matching depends on the glob's literal path pattern, not on the word "api" appearing somewhere in a path, so server/api/ is not covered.
Not “Yes, but only once the new files have been committed to version con…” — Commit status has no bearing on whether a rule's glob matches a path, so committing the files would not cause the rule to apply.
Not “No, because rules never apply to any directory that didn't exist wh…” — Rules are not restricted to directories that existed at creation time. The issue is that this directory is not covered by the listed patterns.

questions.q: A skill at .claude/skills/design-phase/SKILL.md uses context: fork to keep a long back-and-forth about architecture options out of the main conversation, and returns a final structured proposal as its result. Does the main session also retain the intermediate questions, dead ends, and exploratory reasoning that happened inside that fork?
options: Yes — context: fork only changes what's displayed; all the underlying reasoning is still part of the session
No — the fork's exploratory reasoning stays isolated to keep the main session's context clean; only the final result the skill actually returns comes back
Only if the skill happens to summarize its own reasoning as part of that final output
Yes, but only after a manual step re-merges the fork's context into the main thread
questions.explain:
context: fork exists specifically to keep a skill's exploratory reasoning out of the main session's context; only the final result the skill actually returns comes back, not the intermediate questions and dead ends that led to it.
Not “Yes — context: fork only changes what's displayed; all the underl…” — context: fork does more than change what is displayed. The fork's intermediate reasoning is kept out of the main session's context.
Not “Only if the skill happens to summarize its own reasoning as part of…” — The main session does not retain the fork's reasoning even without a summary. Only the final result the skill returns comes back.
Not “Yes, but only after a manual step re-merges the fork's context into…” — No manual step is needed to keep the fork's context out, and no re-merge of the fork's reasoning happens automatically either.

questions.q: A task is described simply as "remove unused dependencies from package.json and update three import statements." On investigation, it turns out this actually means reconciling 15 separate package removals with genuinely competing priorities from eight different teams that depend on different subsets of them. Given that complexity, what's the more appropriate approach?
options: Direct execution — dependency removal is inherently a simple, mechanical task
Plan mode — the real work here is resolving competing priorities and removal order across teams, which is a design question that benefits from being worked out before any file gets touched
Direct execution, switching to plan mode only if something unexpected comes up along the way
Neither — this specific kind of cross-team coordination is out of scope for Claude Code entirely
questions.explain:
Once the real shape of the task turns out to be reconciling genuinely competing priorities across eight teams, that's exactly the kind of design question plan mode is suited to work through before any file gets touched — a very different situation from the surface-level "update three imports" framing the task started with.
Not “Direct execution — dependency removal is inherently a simple, mecha…” — Calling dependency removal inherently mechanical ignores that reconciling competing priorities across eight teams is a design question.
Not “Direct execution, switching to plan mode only if something unexpect…” — Waiting for something unexpected before planning risks changing files in the wrong order across teams, when the complexity is already known.
Not “Neither — this specific kind of cross-team coordination is out of s…” — Cross-team coordination is not out of scope for Claude Code. Plan mode is well suited to working through such a design question.

questions.q: A /generate-tests skill produces new test files with a lot of repeated boilerplate — fixture setup, mock definitions, assertion patterns — duplicated nearly identically across runs. Re-invoking it with an added instruction to "avoid boilerplate" doesn't change the output. What's the most direct fix?
options: Include the team's existing test files as context, and document the available fixtures and standard assertion patterns the team already has in CLAUDE.md
Increase max_tokens so the skill has more room to vary its output
Add one "good" example test at the very start of the prompt as a single few-shot example
Decrease max_tokens to force shorter, simpler generated tests
questions.explain:
Giving the model the team's actual existing tests as context, plus documenting available fixtures and assertion patterns in CLAUDE.md, gives it concrete, specific patterns to reuse instead of reinventing boilerplate each time — which a token-budget change or a single extra example don't reliably provide.
Not “Increase max_tokens so the skill has more room to vary its output” — More max_tokens leaves the model free to reproduce the same boilerplate and does not show it the team's existing patterns.
Not “Add one "good" example test at the very start of the prompt as a si…” — A single example at the start of a prompt gives only one pattern, while the team's real fixtures and assertion styles are what it needs to reuse.
Not “Decrease max_tokens to force shorter, simpler generated tests” — Reducing max_tokens forces shorter output but does not make the model reuse existing fixtures, so boilerplate would remain or be cut mid-test.

questions.q: A validateUser function needs three interdependent checks: the user must be active, must have an assigned role, and that role must pass a whitelist. Across two separate attempts at implementing this, Claude structures the interaction between the three checks differently each time — once checking all three independently, once only checking the role if the user is already active. What's the most effective way to pin down the exact intended behavior?
options: Repeat the requirement more forcefully: "make sure all three conditions are checked consistently"
Provide a small test suite covering every meaningful combination (active/inactive × role-present/missing × role-valid/invalid) and share the actual failures after each attempt
Ask Claude to "be more careful about edge cases this time"
Generate five separate attempts and manually pick whichever looks best
questions.explain:
A small test suite covering every meaningful combination of the three interdependent conditions, with real failures shared back after each attempt, pins down the exact intended behavior far more reliably than repeating the same prose requirement more forcefully or picking a favorite among several blind attempts.
Not “Repeat the requirement more forcefully: "make sure all three condit…” — Repeating the requirement more forcefully leaves the interaction between the checks ambiguous, so the structure can still change between attempts.
Not “Ask Claude to "be more careful about edge cases this time"” — "Be more careful" is vague and does not specify how the three conditions combine, so inconsistent interpretation is likely to continue.
Not “Generate five separate attempts and manually pick whichever looks best” — Choosing among five attempts by hand does not define the intended behaviour and just sorts through inconsistent implementations.

questions.q: Before implementing a cache-eviction strategy in a service the developer has never worked in, they want Claude to first surface open design questions (TTL vs. LRU, single- vs. multi-tier, what triggers invalidation) rather than go straight to an implementation. Which technique fits best?
options: Test-driven iteration, backed by a comprehensive test suite covering cache behavior
The interview pattern — have Claude ask clarifying design questions before proposing any implementation
Plan mode, working from a detailed architectural brief the developer writes upfront
Direct execution, just with a longer and more specific initial prompt
questions.explain:
The interview pattern is built for exactly this situation: a domain unfamiliar enough that the developer can't yet know which tradeoffs (TTL vs. LRU, tiering, invalidation triggers) actually matter, so surfacing those questions before implementation catches gaps a detailed upfront prompt would likely miss.
Not “Test-driven iteration, backed by a comprehensive test suite coverin…” — Test-driven iteration assumes you can already specify the expected behaviour, and that is exactly what the developer is missing in this unfamiliar domain.
Not “Plan mode, working from a detailed architectural brief the develope…” — Plan mode with a developer-written brief depends on the developer already knowing the relevant tradeoffs, which they do not here.
Not “Direct execution, just with a longer and more specific initial prompt” — A longer, more specific prompt is limited by what the developer already knows, so it cannot surface considerations they have not thought of.

questions.q: Your .claude/settings.json has two separate PreToolUse hooks: one matching Write that runs a formatting check, and one matching Edit that runs a type-checking validation. A developer performs an Edit on a file that would fail the formatting check but pass type-checking. Which hook(s) actually run?
options: The formatting hook runs first alphabetically, blocks the call, and type-checking never runs
Both hooks run regardless of which tool was called — formatting is checked, then type-checking
Only the type-checking hook runs, since it matches Edit; the formatting hook is scoped to Write and doesn't fire here at all
Neither hook runs, since hooks are only evaluated for Write, never for Edit
questions.explain:
Hooks are scoped by their matcher; a hook matching Write simply doesn't fire for an Edit call, and vice versa. Since this operation is an Edit, only the type-checking hook (matched to Edit) runs — the formatting hook never gets a chance to block anything here.
Not “The formatting hook runs first alphabetically, blocks the call, and…” — Hooks are scoped by matcher, not ordered alphabetically across tools. The formatting hook matches Write and does not run for an Edit.
Not “Both hooks run regardless of which tool was called — formatting is …” — Hooks do not all run regardless of the tool. Each fires only when its matcher matches the tool being called.
Not “Neither hook runs, since hooks are only evaluated for Write, neve…” — Hooks are evaluated for Edit as well as Write. A hook matching Edit does run, so it is wrong that none fire.

questions.q: A skill at .claude/skills/security-audit/SKILL.md has allowed-tools: ["Read", "Grep"] in its frontmatter, meant to keep it to pure file analysis. Mid-run, it decides it needs to actually execute a quick node --check on a module to confirm it's syntactically importable, and attempts to use Bash. What actually happens when it attempts to use Bash?
options: Bash isn't in the skill's allowed-tools list, so the skill cannot invoke a tool outside that set
Nothing in the skill blocks it: allowed-tools only pre-approves the listed tools, so Bash stays callable and the session's permission settings decide whether it prompts or runs
Bash is categorically disallowed inside any skill, regardless of configuration
allowed-tools is ignored entirely, so Bash runs at once with no permission check, whatever the permission settings say
questions.explain:
allowed-tools means “tools Claude can use without asking permission during the turn that invokes this skill”. It does not restrict which tools are available: every tool remains callable, and your permission settings still govern tools that are not listed, so Bash is subject to the normal permission flow. To actually block it, use disallowed-tools or a deny rule.
Not “Bash isn't in the skill's allowed-tools list…” — this is the near-miss: it reads the field as a restriction, which it is not.
Not “Bash is categorically disallowed inside any skill…” — Bash is not banned in skills.
Not “allowed-tools is ignored entirely…” — the field does take effect (listed tools skip the prompt), and permission settings still govern Bash, so it does not run unchecked.

questions.q: A developer is deep into a four-hour refactoring session, having created 25+ new utility functions along the way. The session started with an explicit constraint: "every new utility function must include a full parameter/return-type doc comment." Around the three-and-a-half-hour mark, Claude quietly stops following that convention and starts writing bare one-line comments on new utilities instead. The developer doesn't want to restart and lose the accumulated refactoring context. What's the most effective fix?
options: Restart the session to reset context and re-establish the constraint from scratch

Maintain a short scratchpad file stating the doc-comment constraint explicitly, and have Claude check it before writing a new utility, giving the rule a durable anchor outside the flow of an increasingly long conversation
Increase max_tokens so Claude has more room to "remember" the constraint
Repeat the constraint verbally in the chat with extra emphasis whenever it's noticed slipping
questions.explain:
A short scratchpad stating the constraint explicitly, checked before writing a new utility, gives the rule a durable anchor outside the conversation's own shifting "salience" — which is what quietly erodes over a long session and is why the convention started slipping around hour three and a half. Restarting throws away the accumulated refactoring context the developer explicitly wants to keep, and repeating the constraint verbally is exactly the kind of reminder that already stopped working once.
Not “Restart the session to reset context and re-establish the constrain…” — Restarting throws away the accumulated refactoring context that the developer explicitly wants to keep.
Not “Increase max_tokens so Claude has more room to "remember" the con…” — max_tokens governs response length and does not help Claude remember a convention given hours earlier.
Not “Repeat the constraint verbally in the chat with extra emphasis when…” — Repeating the constraint with emphasis whenever it slips is the same reminder approach that already stopped working, and gives no durable reference.

questions.q: A research coordinator runs a fixed pipeline — search, then analyze, then synthesize, then report — with no step in between that re-evaluates whether coverage is actually adequate. On topically broad requests (e.g., "AI regulation across multiple jurisdictions"), the resulting reports keep coming back with real regional gaps, even though every individual subagent completed its assigned piece without error. What architectural change addresses this?
options: Give the search subagent access to more search tools so it can generate extra results upfront
After synthesis, have the coordinator evaluate whether real coverage gaps remain and, if so, conditionally spawn targeted follow-up searches before finalizing the report
Simply increase the number of initial parallel search queries at the start
Let each subagent decide on its own whether to spawn additional follow-up investigations
questions.explain:
Adding an explicit coverage check after synthesis — and conditionally spawning follow-up searches only when real gaps remain — is what lets the pipeline adapt to what it actually finds, instead of running the same fixed sequence regardless of whether the topic turned out to need more regional coverage than initially planned.
Not “Give the search subagent access to more search tools so it can gene…” — More search tools upfront do not add a check on whether coverage is adequate, so regional gaps could still remain after a fixed pipeline.
Not “Simply increase the number of initial parallel search queries at th…” — More parallel initial queries do not tell the coordinator which regions are actually missing, so gaps may remain.
Not “Let each subagent decide on its own whether to spawn additional fol…” — Letting each subagent spawn follow-ups on its own removes central evaluation of overall coverage, which only the coordinator can judge.

questions.q: A coordinator runs three subagents in parallel — web search, document analysis, and source synthesis — then passes all three outputs into a single, very long block of text for a final synthesis pass. The resulting report draws heavily on the search and document-analysis findings, but almost never references the source-synthesis subagent's output, even though that subagent completed successfully and returned substantive material. What's the most likely cause?
options: The third subagent's output was never actually included in what was sent to the final synthesis step
A separate follow-up turn is required before synthesis can incorporate a third input source

The third subagent's findings ended up buried in the middle of a very long combined prompt, with nothing structurally marking them as important, so they got less attention than the material at the start and end
The document-analysis subagent's output silently overwrote the third subagent's data before synthesis ran
questions.explain:
When several subagents' outputs are concatenated into one very long prompt with nothing marking which parts matter, material buried in the middle predictably gets less attention than what's near the start or end — the classic "lost in the middle" effect, not a case of the data having been dropped or overwritten or needing an extra turn.
Not “The third subagent's output was never actually included in what was…” — The scenario says the third subagent returned substantive material that was passed on, so nothing indicates it was left out of the input.
Not “A separate follow-up turn is required before synthesis can incorpor…” — No extra turn is needed for synthesis to take in a third source, and the material was present in the combined text.
Not “The document-analysis subagent's output silently overwrote the thir…” — Nothing in the pipeline overwrites one subagent's data with another's, so silent overwriting does not explain the omission.

questions.q: A coordinator has access to a discover_available_sources tool that returns a static, pre-curated catalog of about 150 approved research sources. In practice, the coordinator calls this tool near the start of almost every research task just to see what's available, before doing anything else — an extra round-trip nearly every time, for content that barely changes. What's the most appropriate fix?
options: Improve the tool's description so its purpose is clearer
Expose the source catalog as an MCP **resource** instead of a tool, since it's read-only reference material the coordinator needs to see, not an action the model is actively deciding to take
Force tool_choice so the discovery call always happens as the very first step
Hard-code the entire source list directly into the coordinator's system prompt
questions.explain:
A largely static, read-only catalog that exists to be looked up — not acted on — is exactly what MCP resources are for; exposing it that way removes the tool-call decision and round-trip entirely, rather than just making the tool's description clearer or forcing when the call happens.
Not “Improve the tool's description so its purpose is clearer” — A clearer description does not remove the round trip. The agent would still call the tool near the start to see the same static list.
Not “Force tool_choice so the discovery call always happens as the ver…” — Forcing the discovery call to happen first makes the unnecessary round-trip mandatory rather than removing it.
Not “Hard-code the entire source list directly into the coordinator's sy…” — Hard-coding 150 sources into the system prompt bloats every request and requires editing the prompt whenever the catalogue changes.

questions.q: A coordinator delegates "research recent regulatory changes on topic X" to one subagent and "research historical precedent for topic X" to a second subagent, reusing the exact same prompt template for both and only swapping the topic phrase. The "recent changes" report later turns out to reference "established historical patterns" and "prior precedent," despite being explicitly scoped to recent developments only. What's the most likely cause?
options: The two subagents share some kind of common memory pool that lets findings bleed between them

Reusing the identical prompt template for both tasks carries unintended thematic association from one into the other — the shared phrasing, not any shared state, is what's pulling "precedent" language into the recent-changes report
The coordinator's own system prompt wasn't specific enough to keep the two request types apart
The two delegations should have run sequentially instead of in parallel
questions.explain:
With no shared state between the two delegations, what's actually carrying "precedent" language into the recent-changes report is the identical prompt template itself — the phrasing pattern, not any shared memory — pulling in an unintended thematic association. The fix is differentiating how each task is framed, not adjusting the coordinator's own system prompt or the parallel-vs-sequential structure.
Not “The two subagents share some kind of common memory pool that lets f…” — The subagents are separate invocations and nothing indicates a shared memory pool, so shared state is not what carried the language across.
Not “The coordinator's own system prompt wasn't specific enough to keep …” — The coordinator's own system prompt is not the cause. The identical per-task prompt template is what created the thematic bleed.
Not “The two delegations should have run sequentially instead of in para…” — Running the delegations sequentially would not remove the shared phrasing that caused the association, so the structure is not the cause.

questions.q: In a coordinator's pipeline, the report-generation subagent is meant to run only after the synthesis subagent has returned its findings — but the pipeline itself has no runtime mechanism enforcing that order, only an implicit assumption. During testing, report generation occasionally starts before synthesis has actually completed, producing polished-looking sections with citations that can't be verified against anything synthesis was supposed to have vetted. What's the most reliable way to prevent this?
options: Add explicit ordering language to both subagents' own system prompts
Add a hook on the coordinator's dispatch step that blocks a report-generation call from proceeding until synthesis's result is actually present
Add several few-shot examples showing the two steps happening in the correct order
Increase the coordinator's context window so it "remembers" the intended order better
questions.explain:
A hook that actually blocks the report-generation dispatch until synthesis's result exists enforces the ordering deterministically; prompt-level ordering language, few-shot examples, or a bigger context window are all still just probabilistic nudges toward an order the pipeline itself doesn't actually guarantee.
Not “Add explicit ordering language to both subagents' own system prompts” — Ordering language in the subagents' prompts is advisory, so report generation can still start early when nothing enforces the sequence.
Not “Add several few-shot examples showing the two steps happening in th…” — Few-shot examples only suggest the correct order and do not stop an early dispatch, so the problem can still occur.
Not “Increase the coordinator's context window so it "remembers" the int…” — A larger window gives the coordinator no mechanism to enforce order and does not change when dispatch actually happens.

questions.q: A synthesis subagent frequently needs to verify simple facts mid-synthesis — a publication date, an author's name, a cited statistic — and today every single one of these routes through the coordinator to a full search subagent and back, even though roughly 85% of these checks are genuinely simple lookups. The remaining 15% require real investigative depth. What's the best fix?
options: Give the synthesis subagent unrestricted access to the same full search and analysis tools every other subagent uses
Give the synthesis subagent one narrowly scoped verify_fact-style tool for the common, simple case, while still routing the rarer, genuinely complex checks through the coordinator
Batch every verification and run them all in one dedicated pass only after synthesis has otherwise finished
Drop fact verification from the synthesis step entirely to reduce latency
questions.explain:
A narrowly scoped verification tool lets the common, simple 85% of checks resolve locally without a coordinator round-trip, while the rarer, genuinely complex 15% still get routed through the coordinator where that overhead is actually justified. Full tool access for synthesis reintroduces the coordination and scope problems scoped tools exist to avoid.
Not “Give the synthesis subagent unrestricted access to the same full se…” — Unrestricted access to the full search tools lets the synthesis agent drift out of its role and brings back the coordination issues scoped tools avoid.
Not “Batch every verification and run them all in one dedicated pass onl…” — Running all verifications at the end delays catching mistakes and does not remove the round trip for the many simple checks.
Not “Drop fact verification from the synthesis step entirely to reduce l…” — Dropping fact verification removes quality control instead of making it cheaper, so errors in dates and names reach the report.

questions.q: A search subagent times out partway through and returns structured context: "provider timeout, transient, retryable, 60 of an expected 150 results collected." The coordinator now has to decide whether to return the partial 60 results, retry, or escalate to a human. What should actually drive that decision?
options: Always return the partial results immediately, since some information beats none
Always escalate, since any incomplete research inherently needs a human to weigh in

Judge whether the 60 results already collected are enough to satisfy what the user actually asked for; if the missing 90 would plausibly change the conclusions, retry or escalate instead of quietly returning a report built on an incomplete picture
Keep retrying indefinitely until the full 150 results are eventually collected
questions.explain:
Whether to return partial results, retry, or escalate should depend on whether the 60 already-collected results are actually enough to answer what the user asked — not a blanket rule to always return whatever exists, always escalate, or retry forever regardless of diminishing returns.
Not “Always return the partial results immediately, since some informati…” — Always returning partial results would present 60 of 150 results as complete even when the missing ones could change the conclusions.
Not “Always escalate, since any incomplete research inherently needs a h…” — Always escalating treats every incomplete result as needing a human, though the collected 60 may be enough to answer the user.
Not “Keep retrying indefinitely until the full 150 results are eventuall…” — Retrying indefinitely ignores diminishing returns and may block the report forever on a provider that stays down.

questions.q: A document-analysis subagent hits transient errors (timeouts, rate limits) reasonably often, and the coordinator's current policy is simply "retry once, then fail the whole run." As a result, roughly 8–10% of research runs fail outright because of one subagent's temporary hiccup. What's a more effective error-recovery design here?
options: Retry every subagent indefinitely until it eventually succeeds, no matter how long that takes
Use a graduated retry policy with exponential backoff (e.g., 100ms, then 500ms, then 2s) up to a small fixed attempt limit, and only then escalate or continue with a documented partial result
Remove retries entirely and fail the run immediately on the very first transient error
Always escalate any transient error straight to a human without attempting any recovery first
questions.explain:
A graduated backoff-and-retry-limit policy handles the realistic middle ground between giving up too easily and retrying forever regardless of cost — it gives genuinely transient failures a real chance to resolve without letting one subagent's hiccup indefinitely stall the whole pipeline.
Not “Retry every subagent indefinitely until it eventually succeeds, no …” — Retrying indefinitely lets one subagent stall the whole pipeline, with no limit on time or cost.
Not “Remove retries entirely and fail the run immediately on the very fi…” — Failing on the first transient error is exactly the policy that already causes 8-10% of runs to fail from brief hiccups.
Not “Always escalate any transient error straight to a human without att…” — Escalating every transient error to a human without any recovery attempt wastes human time on problems backoff would usually fix.

questions.q: A synthesis pass works through 50 research documents in one long invocation to build a report outline. Reviewers notice a clear pattern: the first 15 sources are cited with real specificity (exact dates, study design, sample sizes), while by document 40 the synthesis is only extracting broad, generic themes. Early report sections are well-supported; later ones are coherent but noticeably vaguer about their sources. What's the most effective architectural fix?
options: Increase the context window so the model can hold onto specificity across all 50 documents at once

Split synthesis into two phases: a "map" phase that extracts detailed, specific claims from each source independently, followed by a "reduce" phase that reconciles and synthesizes across those per-source outputs
Simply process fewer source documents per run, trimming to whatever the model's effective attention span seems to be
Have the model attach a confidence score to each claim and drop everything below a cutoff from the final report
questions.explain:
Splitting into a "map" phase (detailed, per-source extraction, each source getting full attention on its own) and a "reduce" phase (synthesizing across those already-detailed outputs) directly counters the attention tapering that a single 50-document pass produces. A bigger context window doesn't stop attention from tapering within it, and simply processing fewer documents or filtering by a confidence score after the fact don't address why detail degrades as the pass goes on.
Not “Increase the context window so the model can hold onto specificity …” — A larger window does not stop attention from tapering across 50 documents in a single pass, so later sources would still be treated vaguely.
Not “Simply process fewer source documents per run, trimming to whatever…” — Trimming the number of documents drops sources from the report and does not fix why detail fades as one long pass continues.
Not “Have the model attach a confidence score to each claim and drop eve…” — Dropping low-confidence claims afterward does not recover specific detail that was never extracted from the later documents.

questions.q: A code-search MCP tool intermittently returns timeouts, but the agent has no way to tell whether a retry is likely to help or whether the underlying query itself is simply malformed — every failure comes back as {"isError": true, "message": "Operation failed"}. As a result, the agent sometimes retries a hopeless malformed query indefinitely, and sometimes gives up too early on a call that would have succeeded with one more attempt. What's the most direct fix?
options: Add an internal timeout to the tool itself so it fails faster on every kind of error
Add errorCategory (e.g. "transient" vs. "validation") and an isRetryable boolean to the tool's error responses, so the agent has an actual basis for deciding whether to retry
Remove the tool and have the agent fall back to Grep instead
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the agent to "always retry timeouts, never retry validation errors"
questions.explain:
An errorCategory plus an isRetryable flag gives the agent an actual signal to reason from, rather than treating every failure identically — which is what's currently causing it to sometimes retry a hopeless malformed query forever and sometimes give up on a call that would have succeeded with one more attempt.
Not “Add an internal timeout to the tool itself so it fails faster on ev…” — A shorter internal timeout makes the tool fail faster but does not tell the agent whether a failure is worth retrying.
Not “Remove the tool and have the agent fall back to Grep instead” — Removing the tool loses the capability, and falling back to Grep does not fix the missing retry signal for other tools.
Not “Add a system-prompt instruction telling the agent to "always retry …” — A prompt instruction to retry timeouts only cannot work when the agent receives no information saying which failure is a timeout.

questions.q: A list_available_migrations MCP tool returns a catalog of known database migrations. An agent calls it near the start of nearly every migration-related task just to see what's available, before doing any real analysis — an extra round-trip each time for content that's largely static within a session. What's the most efficient fix?
options: Remove the tool from the agent's available tools and require the migration to be named explicitly upfront in every request
Expose the available migrations as an MCP **resource** the agent can read directly, without spending a tool-call decision on pure discovery
Merge every migration-related tool into one larger, more general tool
Cache the tool's result in CLAUDE.md so at least the second call within a session can be skipped
questions.explain:
A largely static catalog that exists purely to be discovered, not acted on, is exactly the case MCP resources are meant for — the agent can read it directly without spending a tool-use decision on pure discovery, which merging or caching into CLAUDE.md don't actually eliminate.
Not “Remove the tool from the agent's available tools and require the mi…” — Requiring migrations to be named upfront removes useful discovery and forces users to know what exists, instead of making the catalogue cheap to read.
Not “Merge every migration-related tool into one larger, more general tool” — Merging migration tools into one bigger tool still costs a decision and round trip, so the discovery cost remains.
Not “Cache the tool's result in CLAUDE.md so at least the second call …” — A CLAUDE.md cache still depends on an extra step to reuse, goes stale silently, and does not eliminate the first discovery call.

questions.q: An MCP server offers list_all_tasks (returns every task in the system) and search_tasks (filters by keyword). Agents sometimes still reach for list_all_tasks on large task inventories when search_tasks would clearly serve better — most often on genuinely ambiguous requests like "find tasks updated in the last week." The team has already rewritten both descriptions with explicit use/non-use guidance and example queries, and the remaining mistakes are concentrated in exactly these edge cases. What's the next lever to try?
options: Remove list_all_tasks from the toolset entirely
Add 2–3 few-shot examples with explicit reasoning showing correct tool selection specifically for these ambiguous, edge-case queries
Rename search_tasks to something that sounds more appealing
Force tool_choice so search_tasks is always selected regardless of the request
questions.explain:
Once description-level fixes have already been applied and the remaining mistakes are concentrated in genuinely ambiguous edge cases, few-shot examples with explicit reasoning are the next lever — well short of removing a legitimate tool or forcing selection regardless of fit.
Not “Remove list_all_tasks from the toolset entirely” — Removing list_all_tasks takes away a legitimate tool needed for cases where listing everything is right, rather than improving choice at the edges.
Not “Rename search_tasks to something that sounds more appealing” — Renaming to sound more appealing does not teach the model how to choose in ambiguous cases, so mistakes would continue.
Not “Force tool_choice so search_tasks is always selected regardless…” — Forcing search_tasks every time would break cases where listing all tasks is the correct choice.

questions.q: An MCP tool compute_code_metrics bundles three distinct capabilities — complexity scoring, test-coverage percentage, and dependency counting — behind one generic description that lists all three. A much lighter, purpose-built count_functions tool also exists for the narrower job of just counting functions, and is meaningfully faster for that specific need. Logs show agents reaching for the heavier, generic tool even for requests the lightweight tool would answer just fine. What's the issue, and the fix?
options: compute_code_metrics is simply too slow and should be deprecated

The generic tool's description gives no signal about when a narrower, faster tool would serve better, so it reads as the safe general-purpose default; the fix is making that boundary explicit in the descriptions
The model needs more few-shot examples covering this exact case
The two tools should be merged into a single combined tool
questions.explain:
A generic description that never mentions a faster, narrower alternative reads as "use me, I'm the safe default" by omission; making that boundary explicit in the description is the direct fix, ahead of deprecating the tool, adding more examples for a problem that's really about missing information, or merging the two.
Not “compute_code_metrics is simply too slow and should be deprecated” — Deprecating the heavier tool removes a legitimate capability, when the issue is that nothing tells the agent when the lighter tool is enough.
Not “The model needs more few-shot examples covering this exact case” — Few-shot examples address a different gap. The generic description lacks information about narrower alternatives, which description changes can supply.
Not “The two tools should be merged into a single combined tool” — Merging the lightweight tool into the heavy one removes the faster option, which defeats the purpose of having it.

questions.q: An MCP tool fetch_repository_metadata returns a repo's package.json contents, top-level README, and directory-tree structure — data that essentially never changes within a session. A productivity agent calls it near the start of almost every codebase-exploration task, adding latency to every single session even though the underlying data was already fetched the last time. What's a more efficient design here?
options: Embed the metadata directly into the system prompt for every session
Cache the metadata inside the agent's CLAUDE.md file
Expose the repository metadata as an MCP **resource** instead of a tool, so it can be referenced directly without a tool-call decision each time
Require developers to paste the metadata into their initial request manually
questions.explain:
Data that's effectively static within a session and exists to be referenced, not acted on, belongs behind an MCP resource rather than a tool — removing the repeated round-trip cost that embedding in the system prompt, caching in CLAUDE.md, or manual developer input don't actually solve as cleanly.
Not “Embed the metadata directly into the system prompt for every session” — Embedding metadata in every system prompt adds tokens to each session and has to be updated whenever the repo changes.
Not “Cache the metadata inside the agent's CLAUDE.md file” — Caching in CLAUDE.md makes a hand-maintained copy that goes stale and is not designed for reference data that should be read on demand.
Not “Require developers to paste the metadata into their initial request…” — Requiring developers to paste metadata into every request pushes repeated manual work onto people and is easy to forget.

questions.q: A code-complexity MCP tool expects a single file path and returns detailed per-function metrics. On a vague request like "analyze the whole codebase," the agent sometimes passes a directory path by mistake, and the tool responds with an enormous combined JSON blob covering every file in that tree — overwhelming the context window and burying whatever signal actually mattered. What's the best way to prevent this?
options: Validate the input inside the tool itself — reject anything that isn't a single file path, with a clear error explaining the expected input shape
Add a PostToolUse hook that trims the response down to top-level metrics after the fact
Expand the tool's description with a warning against passing directories
Remove the tool and require this kind of analysis to be done manually instead
questions.explain:
Validating the input shape inside the tool itself, before the expensive (and here, enormous) operation runs, stops the problem at its actual source; a PostToolUse hook only trims the damage after the huge response has already consumed context and time, and a description-only warning is easy for a vague request to slip past.
Not “Add a PostToolUse hook that trims the response down to top-level …” — A PostToolUse hook trims the response only after the huge output has been produced, so the time and cost of generating it are already spent.
Not “Expand the tool's description with a warning against passing direct…” — A description warning is easy for a vague request to slip past, and it does not stop a directory path from being accepted.
Not “Remove the tool and require this kind of analysis to be done manual…” — Removing the tool gives up useful per-file analysis when a small input check would prevent the problem.

questions.q: A productivity agent has 22 tools available at once — a handful of built-ins plus 19 different MCP integrations for code analysis. Given the narrow task "find memory leaks in this service," evaluation runs show the agent frequently reaching for debugging, profiling, and monitoring tools in various combinations, and only occasionally landing on the one static-analysis tool that's actually best suited to this exact job — a tool that, used alone, produces better results 80% of the time in manual comparisons. What does this pattern suggest, and what's the fix?
options: The prompt needs clearer language specifically about memory-leak detection

Too many simultaneously available, similar-looking tools increase selection complexity; narrowing which tools are actually available for this kind of focused task (rather than leaving all 22 live at once) directly reduces the chance of picking a worse combination
The static-analysis tool's description needs to be more generic so it stands out less
The agent needs a larger context window to properly weigh all 22 options
questions.explain:
With 22 similar-looking tools live at once, narrowing which ones are actually available for a focused task like this one directly reduces the selection space causing the misfires — a more direct fix than better prompting, a more generic description, or hoping a larger context window somehow improves the underlying selection judgment.
Not “The prompt needs clearer language specifically about memory-leak de…” — Prompt language about memory leaks does not reduce the 22 tools competing for selection, so the agent could still pick poorly.
Not “The static-analysis tool's description needs to be more generic so …” — Making the best tool's description more generic would make it less distinguishable, so it would be chosen even less often.
Not “The agent needs a larger context window to properly weigh all 22 op…” — A larger context window does not improve the judgment needed to choose among similar tools, so misselection would continue.

questions.q: An MCP server exposes fetch_openapi_spec (the full spec, on the order of 200KB) and search_api_endpoints (a keyword-filtered search over endpoint definitions, typically a few KB). For a query like "find the endpoint that returns user profiles," logs show the agent frequently pulling the entire spec and searching through it manually, when the dedicated search tool would answer the same question directly. Both tools work correctly and neither is erroring. What's the most direct fix?
options: Remove fetch_openapi_spec since the search tool is more efficient
Make fetch_openapi_spec return only a summary instead of the full document
Sharpen search_api_endpoints's description to explicitly explain when it's the better choice over fetching the whole spec, with example queries it handles well
Raise the model's temperature to encourage broader tool exploration
questions.explain:
Making search_api_endpoints's description explicitly state when it beats fetching the entire spec is the direct fix for this kind of under-selection; removing the full-spec tool breaks legitimate cases that need it, and shrinking its response or raising temperature don't address why the search tool isn't being reached for in the first place.
Not “Remove fetch_openapi_spec since the search tool is more efficient” — Removing fetch_openapi_spec breaks cases that really do need the whole spec, and it does not explain why search was passed over.
Not “Make fetch_openapi_spec return only a summary instead of the full…” — Shrinking the full-spec tool's response changes what it returns without telling the agent that the search tool is the better choice for this query.
Not “Raise the model's temperature to encourage broader tool exploration” — Higher temperature adds randomness to tool choice and does not teach the agent which tool fits endpoint lookups.

questions.q: A generic refactor_code tool handles three unrelated jobs — renaming symbols globally, restructuring module boundaries, and updating dependency declarations — and CI/CD runs occasionally apply the wrong one of the three (e.g., a symbol-rename operation gets applied where a module-boundary restructure was actually needed, causing cascading breakage). The team splits it into three purpose-specific tools: rename_symbols, restructure_modules, update_dependencies. To further reduce the odds of the wrong tool being applied to the wrong kind of change specifically in CI/CD, what should also be added?
options: A PreToolUse hook that inspects which of the three new tools is being invoked together with its target path, and blocks the call if that combination doesn't make sense for the kind of change actually being made (e.g., blocking a rename_symbols call whose target sits inside a migrations directory)
Set tool_choice to force one specific tool for every CI/CD invocation, regardless of task
Increase max_tokens so the agent has more room to reason before choosing
Move all refactoring guidance out of CLAUDE.md and into a custom /refactor skill that must be invoked manually every time
questions.explain:
A PreToolUse hook that inspects the specific tool being called together with its target path is what can actually block a mismatched combination (like a rename operation aimed at a migrations directory) before it executes — this is a real, path-aware enforcement mechanism, unlike .claude/rules/, which scopes what *guidance text* loads for matching files but has no ability to restrict which *tools* are available based on path. Forcing one tool globally via tool_choice would break the other two legitimate use cases, and more reasoning room or a manually-invoked skill don't add any actual enforcement.
Not “Set tool_choice to force one specific tool for every CI/CD invoca…” — Forcing one tool for every CI/CD run would block the other two legitimate operations, so it breaks valid refactoring jobs.
Not “Increase max_tokens so the agent has more room to reason before c…” — More max_tokens gives the model room to produce text but no enforcement that a rename tool is not applied to the wrong kind of target.
Not “Move all refactoring guidance out of CLAUDE.md and into a custom …” — A manually invoked skill depends on someone remembering to use it, and it does not block a mismatched tool and target path combination.

questions.q: A coordinator splits codebase exploration across several subagents, each with Read, Grep, and its own specialized MCP tools. When something goes wrong, the three subagents report failures in three different shapes: one returns structured JSON with error_type/is_recoverable fields, another returns free-text error prose, and a third returns an empty result set marked as a plain success. The coordinator's recovery logic can't reliably decide whether to retry, escalate, or proceed with partial data, because it's working from three incompatible failure formats. What should be fixed first, and why does it span two domains at once?
options: Add normalization logic inside the coordinator that translates all three formats into one internal shape

Standardize what every subagent's underlying tools report on failure — a consistent errorCategory, isRetryable, and actionable context — which is a tool-design fix that in turn is what makes a reliable, consistent coordinator-level retry/escalation policy possible in the first place
Merge all the subagents into one larger agent so there's only one place errors can come from
Give each subagent its own PostToolUse hook that normalizes its own errors before reporting back to the coordinator
questions.explain:
Standardizing what tools report on failure is a tool-design fix (D2) that's the actual prerequisite for a reliable coordinator-level retry/escalation policy (D1) — without a consistent shape to react to, no amount of coordinator-side logic can reliably tell the three formats apart. Merging subagents or pushing normalization down into each subagent separately both sidestep fixing the inconsistency at its source.
Not “Add normalization logic inside the coordinator that translates all …” — Normalising three formats in the coordinator patches over the inconsistency instead of fixing what the underlying tools report on failure.
Not “Merge all the subagents into one larger agent so there's only one p…” — Merging the subagents into one agent avoids the symptom but removes the benefits of separate investigations and does not standardise any tool's errors.
Not “Give each subagent its own PostToolUse hook that normalizes its o…” — A separate hook per subagent normalises errors in three places, rather than fixing the inconsistency at its source in the tools themselves.

questions.q: A CI review agent must only ever perform read operations — Read, Glob, Grep — and should never be able to modify files, run shell commands, or reach out through any MCP tool, no matter who runs it or how the invocation is configured. The team wants this enforced consistently for every developer who clones the repo, not left to individual discipline. What's the most direct mechanism?
options: Add a prominent note in CLAUDE.md instructing Claude to avoid Write and Bash
Add a broad-matcher PreToolUse hook in .claude/settings.json that intercepts every tool call and manually re-implements the same allow logic each time
Configure permissions in .claude/settings.json so only Read, Glob, and Grep are allowed and everything else is denied (deny rules, or dontAsk mode in CI)
Remove Write, Bash, and every MCP tool from the project's tool registry entirely
questions.explain:
Configuring .claude/settings.json permissions so only the three read-only tools are allowed, with everything else denied (deny rules, or dontAsk mode in CI, which auto-denies anything that would otherwise prompt), is a declarative, version-controlled restriction every developer's session inherits automatically — more direct and more maintainable than reimplementing the same allow logic inside a hook, a prompt note that depends on the model following it, or physically stripping tools from the whole project's registry.
Not “Add a prominent note in CLAUDE.md instructing Claude to avoid `Wr…” — A CLAUDE.md note is advisory, so Claude could still use Write or Bash and nothing enforces the read-only limit.
Not “Add a broad-matcher PreToolUse hook in .claude/settings.json th…” — A broad PreToolUse hook that re-implements allow logic is more complicated and error-prone than declaring permissions directly.
Not “Remove Write, Bash, and every MCP tool from the project's tool …” — Stripping tools from the whole project's registry affects every other use of the repo, which is far broader than a read-only review setup.

questions.q: A team runs five review agents in parallel across a large monorepo, each covering a different subsystem, then merges all five sets of findings into one consolidated PR comment. Which specific design choice here is what actually prevents the "a session reviewing its own generated code" bias?
options: Running the analyses in parallel, since parallel work is inherently more thorough than sequential work
Each of the five review agents is its own fully independent Claude Code invocation, carrying no context from whatever session originally generated the code under review
Consolidating the five sets of findings afterward, which lets duplicate issues get filtered out
Using JSON output format, which makes findings more reliable regardless of how the sessions themselves are structured
questions.explain:
What actually removes the generation-reasoning bias is that each of the five review agents is a fully independent invocation carrying no context from whatever session wrote the code in the first place — parallelism alone doesn't provide that independence, and neither does deduplicating findings afterward or the choice of output format.
Not “Running the analyses in parallel, since parallel work is inherently…” — Parallel execution makes the reviews faster, not independent of the generating session, so it does not remove the self-review bias.
Not “Consolidating the five sets of findings afterward, which lets dupli…” — Merging and deduplicating findings after the fact has no effect on whether each reviewer was biased by the code's generating session.
Not “Using JSON output format, which makes findings more reliable regard…” — JSON output improves the format of results but does nothing about whether the reviewing sessions share reasoning with the generator.

questions.q: A review finding schema defines {"violation_type": ..., "description": ..., "remediation": ...}. Every finding validates against the schema successfully, but in practice, proposed fixes routinely end up written into description while remediation gets a vague one-liner like "add validation" — exactly backwards from what each field is meant to hold. The model clearly understands the JSON structure itself. What's the actual problem here?
options: The fields should be marked required when they're currently optional; tightening that constraint will fix the mix-up

The model understands the shape of the schema but not the intended purpose of each individual field; adding 2–3 few-shot examples showing correct field assignment per violation type teaches that distinction directly
An evidence_required list should be added to force more precision automatically
Force tool_choice onto the findings tool to remove any remaining ambiguity
questions.explain:
The model already produces schema-valid JSON, so the problem isn't structural — it's that the model hasn't internalized which content belongs in which field. A few concrete field-assignment examples per violation type teach that distinction directly, which tightening required-ness, adding an unrelated list field, or forcing tool choice don't address.
Not “The fields should be marked required when they're currently optiona…” — The fields are filled and validate already. Marking them required would not tell the model which content belongs in which field.
Not “An evidence_required list should be added to force more precision…” — An evidence_required list adds another field and does not teach the model the purpose of description versus remediation.
Not “Force tool_choice onto the findings tool to remove any remaining …” — Forcing tool_choice only guarantees the tool is called. The model already calls it, so it does not fix field misassignment.

questions.q: Over three sprints, the "possible inconsistency in error-handling patterns" finding category has a 35% developer dismissal rate, while actual bug findings sit under 5%. The prompt already says "only report high-confidence issues." What's the most effective next step to protect developer trust in the review overall?
options: Add even stronger wording: "be even more conservative about pattern consistency"

Temporarily disable the specific "inconsistency" category, keep the well-performing categories (bugs, crashes, security) active, and only bring it back once its criteria have been tightened and re-measured
Lower the model's temperature to make output more deterministic
Require developers to write a detailed justification every time they dismiss a comment
questions.explain:
Temporarily pulling the one category driving nearly all the dismissals — while leaving the well-performing categories active — protects trust in the parts of the review that are actually working, and buys room to fix that category's criteria properly. Stronger wording and a lower temperature haven't moved this kind of false-positive rate before and aren't likely to now; requiring justification for every dismissal adds friction without addressing the underlying noise.
Not “Add even stronger wording: "be even more conservative about pattern…” — Stronger conservative wording is a vague instruction that has not worked, since the prompt already asks for high-confidence issues only.
Not “Lower the model's temperature to make output more deterministic” — Lowering temperature does not tighten what the category counts as an issue, so the dismissal rate would not drop.
Not “Require developers to write a detailed justification every time the…” — Requiring justification for every dismissal adds developer friction and does not fix the noisy category driving the dismissals.

questions.q: Your team wants materially different review standards for code PRs (correctness, performance, security) versus documentation-only PRs (accuracy, link validity, tone), but both currently load the exact same root CLAUDE.md, so doc-only PRs end up getting flagged with irrelevant guidance about concurrency and database migrations. Where should the code-specific guidance move so it only loads when actual code files are involved?
options: A .claude/rules/code-standards.md file with paths frontmatter scoped to source file patterns (e.g. src/**/*.{js,ts}), so it only loads when those files are actually being touched
Two separate root files, code-review-CLAUDE.md and docs-review-CLAUDE.md, with CI deciding which one to load based on PR labels
Move the code standards into an MCP tool the model can optionally call if it thinks it's relevant
Leave everything in the root CLAUDE.md and trust the model to disregard whatever doesn't apply
questions.explain:
